question.prompt: An envelope contains eight bills: \(2\) ones, \(2\) fives, \(2\) tens, and \(2\) twenties. Two bills are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that their sum is \(\$20\) or more?

solutions.explanation:
Treat the eight physical bills as distinct, even when their denominations agree. There are \(8\cdot7\) possible ordered draws without replacement. Each unordered pair appears in exactly two orders, so there are
\[
\frac{8\cdot7}{2}=28
\]
equally likely pairs.

Any pair containing a \(\$20\) bill qualifies. There are \(2\cdot6=12\) pairs containing exactly one twenty: choose one of the two twenties and one of the six other bills. There is also one pair containing both twenties.

Without a twenty, the only qualifying pair is the pair of tens, whose sum is exactly \(\$20\); every other such pair totals at most \(\$15\). These cases are disjoint and include every qualifying pair. Hence the probability is
\[
\frac{12+1+1}{28}=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
solutions.title: Count qualifying pairs
